meta.title: Who originally recorded "The Girl from Ipanema"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto. Pery Ribeiro’s Odeon record was the song’s first commercial release, out in Brazil in 1963; the Verve version followed in March 1964.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The Girl from Ipanema'?
meta.ogDescription: Pery Ribeiro’s Odeon record was the first commercial release, in Brazil in 1963. Getz and Gilberto taped their version in March 1963 and Verve released it in March 1964.

answer.label: Not a Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto original — Pery Ribeiro’s Odeon record was the first version released, in Brazil, in 1963
answer.originalArtistDates: 1937-2012 · Brazilian bossa nova and MPB singer, son of Dalva de Oliveira and Herivelto Martins
answer.sourceLine: Almost everyone meets this song through the Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto recording, and treats that record as the song’s birth. It isn’t. “Garota de Ipanema” was written in 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim (music) and Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics), performed in public for the first time on 2 August 1962 at the Au Bon Gourmet club in Rio, and the first version to reach the public on a record was the Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro’s, issued by Odeon and collected on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa. Sources disagree on exactly when Ribeiro cut it — English Wikipedia says 1962, its own Pery Ribeiro article says January 1963, and the Instituto Moreira Salles discography dates the session to 26 March 1963 — so the safe claim is the one every source supports: his was the first commercial release, in Brazil, in 1963. Norman Gimbel’s English lyric came afterwards, for the international version. Getz and João Gilberto did not tape their Getz/Gilberto session until 18–19 March 1963, and Verve did not release the album until March 1964.

original.heading: Who released it first
original.label: Odeon (Brazil)
original.released: Issued in Brazil by Odeon in 1963 — the song’s first commercial release — and collected on Ribeiro’s LP Pery é Todo Bossa. The exact dates are contested: Portuguese Wikipedia puts the single out in January 1963, while the Instituto Moreira Salles discography dates the session to 26 March 1963 and places the 78 (Odeon 14869-1) and the LP later that year. Weaker still, the streaming metadata on the album track gives 5 January 1963 with a ℗ 1963 EMI Records Brasil line — back-catalogue data, not a pressing date, and not evidence of when the disc reached Brazilian shops.
original.charted: No US or UK chart placing. It was a domestic Brazilian release sung in Portuguese and never issued into the American market.
original.writer: Antônio Carlos Jobim (music); Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
original.cover: Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto, from the album Getz/Gilberto — recorded 18-19 March 1963 in New York, released by Verve in March 1964. The single edit peaked at number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and won the Grammy for Record of the Year in 1965.

trail: English Wikipedia ↗ states that the first commercial recording was by Pery Ribeiro and dates it to 1962, and credits the music to Jobim, the Portuguese lyric to Vinícius de Moraes and the English lyric to Norman Gimbel. Its own Pery Ribeiro article ↗ disagrees, saying he recorded it “in January 1963 for Odeon”.

Portuguese Wikipedia ↗ gives the Brazilian side and dates the RELEASE, not the session: the Ribeiro (Odeon) and Tamba Trio (Philips) singles “foram lançados ao mesmo tempo em janeiro de 1963”. It also describes the song’s live run at the Au Bon Gourmet club in Rio.

The Instituto Moreira Salles discography ↗ dates Ribeiro’s session to 26 March 1963, with Lírio Panicalli’s string arrangement, issued by Odeon as the 78 rpm 14869-1 and on Pery é Todo Bossa. That is a week after the Getz/Gilberto session, which is why this page claims first RELEASE rather than first session. (The site blocks automated fetches; the details above were read from its indexed text.)

The song’s public première, on 2 August 1962 at the Au Bon Gourmet in Copacabana, was taped by the journalist Walter Silva. That tape — now in the Instituto Moreira Salles collection — is the earliest known recording of the song, but João Gilberto never authorised its release, so it has never been commercially issued.
The Getz/Gilberto entry ↗ dates the famous session to 18-19 March 1963 at A&R Recording Studios and the Verve release to March 1964 — both after Ribeiro’s record was already in Brazilian shops.
A MusicBrainz work entry ↗ ties every version to the same Jobim/de Moraes composition, and its Ribeiro recording carries a 1963 first release on Pery é todo bossa.

authors.name: Pery Ribeiro
authors.heading: Pery Ribeiro
authors.bio: Born Peri Oliveira Martins in Rio de Janeiro in 1937, Ribeiro came from Brazilian musical royalty — his mother was the singer Dalva de Oliveira and his father the songwriter Herivelto Martins. He was one of the first voices of bossa nova on record, and he recorded “Garota de Ipanema” for Odeon in January 1963 — the song’s first commercial release — which landed on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa. He kept singing until his death in Rio in 2012, and Rolling Stone Brasil placed him 64th among the country’s hundred greatest singers ↗.

authors.name: Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto
authors.heading: Stan Getz & Astrud Gilberto
authors.bio: The version the world knows was taped in New York on 18 and 19 March 1963 for the album Getz/Gilberto, with Stan Getz on tenor saxophone, João Gilberto on guitar and vocal, Jobim himself at the piano, and João’s wife Astrud Gilberto singing the English lyric — her recording debut. Verve released it in March 1964; the single reached number 5 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and took the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year, while the album became the first non-American record to win Album of the Year. It is a genuinely great record, and it deserves nearly all of its reputation. The only thing it is not is the first.

authors.name: Jobim, Moraes and Gimbel
authors.heading: Jobim, de Moraes & Gimbel
authors.bio: Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the music at his home near Rua Barão da Torre in Ipanema; the poet and diplomat Vinícius de Moraes wrote the Portuguese lyric. The melody began life for a musical comedy under a different working title before it became the song we know. Norman Gimbel, the American lyricist, supplied the separate English words that Astrud Gilberto sang — which is why the Portuguese and English versions are not translations of one another so much as two lyrics fitted to one tune.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong first record
misattribution.intro: The Getz/Gilberto single is one of the most-played recordings ever made, which is exactly why it gets mistaken for the beginning of the story rather than a chapter of it.

items.why: Recorded in New York on 18-19 March 1963 and released by Verve in March 1964. It reached number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and won the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year — but it was not the first recording.

The Brazilian singer made the first commercially released recording of “Garota de Ipanema”, for Odeon, and it appeared on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa. English Wikipedia dates the recording to 1962, its Pery Ribeiro article to January 1963 and the Instituto Moreira Salles discography to 26 March 1963; what nobody disputes is that his was the first version out on a record.

Portuguese-language sources record a Tamba Trio version issued on Philips at the same moment as Ribeiro’s in January 1963, the two labels releasing together to avoid a dispute.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not why Getz and Gilberto had the hit — it is why the Brazilian original vanished so completely from the story. Part of the answer is that Pery Ribeiro’s record was a domestic Brazilian release on Odeon, sung in Portuguese, made for a Rio audience that already knew the song from the bossa nova circuit. It was never aimed at America and never travelled there.

The other part is that Getz/Gilberto arrived with everything the original lacked: an American label, a saxophone star, an English lyric written specifically for export, and a singer — Astrud Gilberto, at the microphone for the first time in her life — whose unpolished delivery turned out to be exactly the sound the record needed. A Grammy for Record of the Year does the rest. Once a song wins the biggest award in American music, the recording that won it becomes, in the popular mind, the recording that started it.
detailsBody: 1962 — Jobim writes the music and Vinícius de Moraes the Portuguese lyric.

2 August 1962 — the song is performed in public for the first time during the bossa nova run at the Au Bon Gourmet nightclub in Rio. The journalist Walter Silva tapes the show; that tape, the earliest known recording of the song, was never commercially released because João Gilberto did not authorise it, so the first commercial recording remains Ribeiro’s.

1963 — Pery Ribeiro cuts the first commercially released version, for Odeon. The session date is contested: English Wikipedia’s song article says 1962, its Pery Ribeiro article says January 1963, and the Instituto Moreira Salles discography says 26 March 1963.

1963 — the Ribeiro recording is issued in Brazil, on the Odeon 78 rpm 14869-1 and on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa. Portuguese-language sources date the single to January 1963 and note a near-simultaneous Brazilian release by Tamba Trio on Philips, timed to avoid a dispute between the labels.
18-19 March 1963 — Stan Getz, João Gilberto, Astrud Gilberto and Jobim record Getz/Gilberto at A&R Recording Studios in New York, produced by Creed Taylor, using Norman Gimbel’s English lyric.
March 1964 — Verve releases Getz/Gilberto. The single edit reaches number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1965 — “The Girl from Ipanema” wins the Grammy for Record of the Year, and the album wins Album of the Year.
context.pull: Ribeiro got it onto a record first; Verve simply sang it louder, in English, to a bigger room.
